blocks.text: Kilajim 8, 5 states that the creature ארני שרה (Simson reads: אבני שרה) belongs to the animal kind (§. 19); R. Jose held that, like a human being, it defiles the tent after its death.

The older commentators make a fabulous animal of it, which is why we shall return to it once more in the last section of this work (§. 506). Here we treat the view of the more recent commentators. Already Beer Naphtali (in the מחנה כהונה on Rabba Kohelet fol. 99, col. 3) wavers between the natural-historical and the fabulous interpretation; he says: ארני שרה is either an animal that resembles man (i.e., the ape), or a man who grows out of the earth.

Landau (on the Aruch) asserts decidedly that ארני שרה is the chimpanzee (Pithecus Troglodytes; also called Jocko, or Barris), whereas Schwarz (הוצאות הארץ fol. 4, 2) explains the animal as the orang-utan (Pithecus Satyrus, also called Pongo, or man of the woods)*). One may waver between the two [p. 65] views, since telling considerations present themselves for each of them. In favour of the explanation as orang-utan speaks the explanation of the Jerusalem Talmud, which explains ארני שרה by בר נש דטור „man of the mountain“; indeed, the former inhabits the high, wooded mountains in the interior of Borneo, Cochin-China and Malacca, so that it is extremely difficult to catch (Voigt, Lehrb. der Zoologie 1, p. 243), whereas the Jocko lives in the forests of Guiana.
Furthermore, it is indeed the orang-utan and not the chimpanzee that is regarded by Linnaeus as, so to speak, a kind of man and is called Homo troglodytes.

On the other hand, the following speaks in favour of the assumption of the chimpanzee: The word ארני means either lord (from ארון, in the construct state אֲרֹנִי; it would be wrong to read אֲרֹנִי after the form of אבני, as Simson would have it), or man (as Bochart thinks, holding that נ has been confused with מ; Hieroz. P. 2, 4, 13, col. 846). The name is therefore also Gen. masc., and for מטמאוח (she defiles) one must read with Bartenoro: מטמא.
The notion of this name is

in any case, however, the resemblance to man, and indeed the Jocko is the most manlike, which is why it is also called the African man of the woods. It also has more intelligence than the Pongo. It builds itself huts out of brushwood against the heat of the sun; it breaks off pieces with which it beats men and elephants; it is even said to carry off Negro women and keep them in captivity for years, and it can be trained to be a skilful and obedient servant (Voigt l. c. 1, p. 240). Further, in favour of this view is the fact that the Talmudists very probably had more knowledge of African than of Further-Indian animals. Since, then, just as many reasons can be adduced for as against the one view and the other, the choice between the two must for the time being still remain to be determined.

The Midrash (l. c.) seems either not to have known of the training of this animal, and of apes in general, or at any rate not to have rated it very highly. With reference to the scriptural verse (Koh. 6, 11): „There are many things that increase vanity“, it says the following: For example, those who rear apes, cats, great weasels (§. 129), Adone Sadeh and seals—what enjoyment do they have of them?“ In the Jalkut Schimoni (part 2, fol. 186, 1) only apes and cats are mentioned, and in place of the other animals pigs are mentioned. In the Midrasch Jelamdenu (Pirschat Schelach [p. 66] lecha) only apes and dogs are cited.
The sense of all these Midrashim, however, is that all the animals mentioned are to be regarded as useless because they may not be eaten.

As for the second reading אבני שרה, the poet (Job. 5, 23) is said to have had our animal in mind when he says: „With the אבני שרה (stones of the field) you shall have a covenant, and with the beasts of the field peace.“ But what sense would the meaning of stones give here? Probably אבני here is meant to correspond to the Arabic ابناء [abnāʾ] (pl. of ابن [ibn], son); the א would then be regarded as an Aleph prostheticum, as in אצערה, אורוע etc., and the sense would be: „sons of the field“, which would mean as much as our „man of the woods“.

קופא (Nedarim 50b) and קוף (Bechoroth 8a). Greek Κῆβος [Kēbos] and Κεῖπος [Keipos]. Rashi on the second passage: שינייא, i.e., Singe. Maimuni (Kilajim 8, 6): *)נקרא בלשון ערב קדר „is called in Arabic: Kerdon“, and the same (Idaim 1, 5): הקוף בערב קדר והוא אשר קוריו אותו במצרים אל נסנ"א בלשין ערב „The ape is in Arabic Kerdon; it is the one that in Egypt is called in Arabic al nisnun.“
Bartenoro (ibid.): חיה ששמה מונ"א „an animal that is called (in Spanish) Mono“.
Pl. קופין (B. Kama 80a) and קופות (probably a misprint) Midr. Rabba Kohelet fol. 99, 3, on which the מחנח כהונה: אפין, i.e. Affen.
